system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-02-02 00:10:00 to 2174-02-03 16:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for right-sided abdominal pain and nausea, occurring four days prior to admission. She has a history of gastric bypass and relies on tube feeds due to poor oral intake and post-surgical hypoglycemia. Initial management included NPO status and IV fluids. A CT scan ruled out bowel obstruction, showing the G-tube in correct position without signs of blockage. Tube feeds were restarted gradually and advanced to her baseline rate of 60 cc/hr, which she tolerated well. Pain and nausea were controlled throughout the stay. She was discharged home with home health services for wound care, continuing rifaximin, sucralfate, lansoprazole, docusate, and PRN Dilaudid. Follow-up was arranged with her surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling dizzy and nauseous. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been feeling lightheaded, especially when I stand up. It started about a week ago. I also feel dehydrated and nauseous, but I haven’t actually vomited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any other symptoms? Chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some palpitations, but no chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how’s your tube feeding been going? Are you tolerating it well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been okay, but I haven’t been drinking much water. I’ve been relying mostly on the tube feeds. I’ve also had some diarrhea the last couple of days, which is unusual for me—I’m usually constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. We’ll check your labs and start you on IV fluids to help with the dehydration. That should also help with the dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I was worried it might be my blood sugar again. I’ve had low sugars before when I don’t eat enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your glucose in the ER—it was 103, which is normal. But we’ll keep an eye on it, especially given your history of hypoglycemia after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. And my incision—when I wretch, it hurts a little there. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The exam shows your wound is healing well—red granulation tissue, no infection. A little discomfort with straining is expected. We’ll make sure it stays clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was also told I might have bacterial overgrowth before. Could that be acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. You’re already on rifaximin, which helps with that. We’ll continue it and see if symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my anxiety—sometimes I feel like my heart races, and I get lightheaded. Could that be part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Anxiety can definitely cause palpitations and dizziness. But we’ve ruled out serious heart issues—the ECG was normal, and your rhythm is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. So, what’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids for a few hours to rehydrate you. We’ll repeat some labs to make sure your electrolytes are balanced. Then, if you’re tolerating water, we’ll discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If things go well, yes. We just want to make sure you’re stable and symptoms are resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat labs look good—kidney function, electrolytes, and glucose are all stable. The IV fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I do feel a bit better. Less dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll try giving you small sips of water to see how you tolerate it. If that goes well, we can plan for discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I restart my tube feeds at home at the usual rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your regular tube feed regimen. Make sure to include extra fluids between feeds to prevent dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I sometimes forget to drink enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Maybe set a reminder. Staying hydrated is key, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been sipping water well and haven’t felt nauseous. Your vitals are stable. I think we’re on track for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my medications? Should I change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Continue all your current meds—lansoprazole, rifaximin, fluoxetine, lorazepam, and the others. They’re important for your stomach, mood, and bowel regularity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel dizzy again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, sit or lie down. Then drink some fluids. If it doesn’t improve, or if you feel worse, come back or call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my follow-up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled to see them soon. They’ll monitor your G-tube, hydration, and overall recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve done well overnight. Still no dizziness or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. I walked to the bathroom fine and drank water without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to stay on top of my fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if anything changes. You’re doing well—just need to stay consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and see you in clinic soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with lightheadedness and nausea, which she had been experiencing for about a week, along with palpitations and recent non-bloody diarrhea—unusual for her as she is typically constipated. She has a complex history including gastric bypass, G-tube dependence, post-surgical hypoglycemia, and prior bacterial overgrowth. In the emergency department, she was found to be dehydrated but stable, with normal glucose, kidney function, and ECG. She was started on IV fluids, which resolved her symptoms. She tolerated oral intake and remained hemodynamically stable throughout her stay. Her medications, including rifaximin and lansoprazole, were continued. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged, advised to maintain hydration and resume normal tube feeding.
